question: Using this FAQ
answer: If you've wondered about how specific card interactions work or when certain game mechanics apply, you're in the right place. Each page walks through common questions with practical examples and references to the official Core Rules Document, helping you understand not just what the ruling is, but why it works that way. Rule numbers link to this site's rendering of the official CRD, and card names link to the gallery. These pages are also handy for sharing in community discussions when the same questions come up.

question: About rule references
answer: Each versioned rulings page shows which Core Rules Document it references, with an "up-to-date" or "outdated" notice at the top. When a page references an older CRD version, all rule number links point to that specific version until the page gets updated. Rule numbers and rules text can change between CRD versions. Remember: the official CRD is always the ultimate authority for Riftbound rules. This FAQ exists to help you learn through examples and explanations, not to replace the official rules.

question: Does Abandoned Hall's ability trigger if the spell is countered?
answer: No. Abandoned Hall's ability triggers "when a player plays a spell," and a countered spell is not considered played. A card is only played once the entire play process has finished in its entirety. [ 350.1 ] Abilities that trigger on playing a card fire when that act has been completed by the card's resolution; [ 419.4.a ] if a game effect prevents resolution — for example because the spell was countered — the card is not considered to have been played and no abilities that trigger on playing cards fire. [ 419.4.a.1 ] This follows directly from what countering does: a countered card is cleared from the chain and is not considered to have been played. [ 425.1.b ]

question: Can a unit moved into or away from Abandoned Hall by a spell be chosen?
answer: Only if it is at Abandoned Hall after the spell fully resolves. A card is only considered "played" once the entire play process has finished, [ 350.1 ] which for spells means after all instructions have been executed and the card is placed in the trash. Abandoned Hall's triggered ability therefore fires after the spell resolves, not when it is placed on the chain. [ 419.4.a ] [ 383.2.c ] By then, a unit moved into Abandoned Hall is present and can be chosen, while a unit moved away no longer qualifies as "a unit they control here."

question: Can a unit replayed here by a spell be chosen by Abandoned Hall's triggered ability?
answer: Yes. Spells like Arcane Shift and Thrill of the Hunt add the unit to the chain as a pending item during their own resolution, pausing its play process while the spell continues. [ 354.2 ] [ 354.3 ] When the spell finishes resolving, it is fully played and Abandoned Hall's triggered ability becomes pending after the unit. [ 350.1 ] [ 419.4.a ] [ 383.2.c ] Because pending items are finalized in the order they were appended, [ 337.1.b ] the unit is finalized and placed on the board first — resolving immediately on finalization [ 337.2 ] — before the triggered ability's target is chosen. By that point the unit is already present at Abandoned Hall and is a valid choice for the buff.

question: Resolution Sequence
answer: Taking Arcane Shift as an example: "Banish a friendly unit" — the unit leaves the board. "then its owner plays it, ignoring its cost" — the unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [ 354.2 ] but its play process pauses while Arcane Shift continues resolving. [ 354.3 ] Arcane Shift finishes resolving and is banished; the spell is now fully played, [ 350.1 ] so Abandoned Hall's triggered ability becomes pending after the unit. [ 419.4.a ] [ 383.2.c ] Required cleanups run before either pending item can be finalized. [ 334.1 ] Once those outstanding tasks are complete, pending items are finalized in the order they were appended. [ 337.1.b ] The unit comes first, resolves immediately upon finalization, [ 337.2 ] and is placed at Abandoned Hall. Abandoned Hall's triggered ability is finalized next; you choose a target, and the replayed unit is now present here as a valid choice. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Does the enemy Dazzling Aurora I take control of with Akshan also trigger at the end of this turn?
answer: No — you gain control of it too late in the turn for its trigger to fire. Dazzling Aurora 's trigger condition is "At the end of your turn." "At" identifies a triggered ability keyed to a specific point in time during the turn sequence [ 383.1 ] — here, the Ending Step, when end-of-turn game effects take place. [ 317.1 ] [ 317.1.a ] A trigger's condition is evaluated once, immediately after that point in time is reached [ 383.2.c ] — it is not re-checked continuously for as long as the game remains in the Ending Phase. After Akshan enters the board, his play effect is added to the chain as a pending item. [ 383.4.a ] [ 383.4.a.2 ] You gain control of the enemy Dazzling Aurora only when that play effect later resolves. At the end of your turn, Dazzling Aurora was still controlled by your opponent, so its controller-relative "your turn" condition did not refer to your turn. By the time you gain control of it, that point in the turn has passed; there's no second check waiting for it later in the phase. It will trigger normally at the end of your future turns, for as long as you continue to control it.

question: What happens when your opponent's Akshan takes control of the gear your Akshan already controls and one or both Akshans die?
answer: Whichever control effect was established most recently determines control of the gear while both effects remain active. Each Akshan's play effect creates a delayed passive ability: "You control it until I leave the board." [ 390.4 ] [ 391 ] These abilities generate continuous effects that change the gear's controller — an inherent trait of every game object. [ 477.1 ] [ 477.1.a ] Since both effects operate in the same layer and neither depends on the other, [ 478 ] they are ordered by timestamp: the earliest-established effect applies first, and the most recently established effect applies last, winning out. [ 480 ] [ 480.1 ] [ 480.3 ] Your opponent's Akshan was played after yours, so it carries the later timestamp — its control effect is the final one applied, and your opponent controls the gear. When an Akshan leaves the board, its "until I leave the board" duration ends and its control effect ceases immediately. The remaining effects are then re-evaluated in timestamp order: Your opponent's Akshan dies : their effect ceases. Only your Akshan's effect remains, giving you control of the gear. Your Akshan dies : your effect ceases. Your opponent's Akshan's effect was already the deciding one — they continue to control the gear unchanged. Both Akshans die : both effects cease. Control reverts to your opponent, since it was their gear to begin with. If the gear is unattached and now finds itself in a base it doesn't belong to, it will be recalled to your opponent's base during the next cleanup. [ 323.7 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: How are targets chosen when playing Alpha Strike?
answer: When finalizing Alpha Strike on the chain, choose the friendly unit, then choose up to one enemy unit at a battlefield per point of its current might. The friendly unit is chosen explicitly as a standard target. The enemy units are targets generated by the split-target instruction. [ 355.14.a ] [ 355.14.b ] [ 355.14.c ] You may choose fewer enemy units than the friendly unit's current might, including zero. [ 355.14.c ] Since each chosen enemy unit is a target of Alpha Strike, Deflect is added as a mandatory additional cost for any of those units that have it during finalization. [ 356.2.a.2 ] [ 809.1.d ] All choices are locked in at finalization and cannot be changed after this step. [ 355.15 ] Example You play Alpha Strike and choose a friendly unit with 4 might. You may then choose up to 4 enemy units at battlefields as the split targets. You choose 3. Those 3 units — and the friendly unit — are all locked in as targets.

question: When is the damage distribution decided?
answer: The distribution of damage across the chosen enemy units is decided at resolution, not at finalization. [ 355.14.e ] The total damage available equals the friendly unit's effective might when Alpha Strike resolves — meaning any Reaction speed buffs or debuffs applied by either player between finalization and resolution will affect the damage pool. [ 359.3.f.2 ] Each chosen target must receive at least 1 damage. [ 355.14.f ] [ 355.14.g ] Beyond that minimum, you may distribute the remaining damage among those targets however you choose, but all available damage must be distributed. Example You chose 3 enemy units at finalization. When Alpha Strike resolves, your friendly unit has 6 might. You must assign at least 1 damage to each of the 3 targets. The remaining 3 damage can go wherever you choose — 4/1/1, 2/2/2, 1/1/4, and so on.

question: What if the chosen friendly unit leaves the board or becomes illegal before Alpha Strike resolves?
answer: It remains legal if it only moves to another board location while remaining a friendly unit; otherwise, Alpha Strike deals no damage. Alpha Strike does not require the chosen friendly unit to be at a particular location. If it moves elsewhere on the board but remains a friendly unit, it is still a legal target and deals damage using its effective might when Alpha Strike resolves. [ 359.3.e.2 ] [ 359.3.f.2 ] If the target changes to a non-board zone, stops being a unit, or stops being friendly, it is illegal as Alpha Strike resolves. [ 359.3.e.2 ] Alpha Strike still resolves, but the illegal target is unaffected and the "its Might" referent returns null, so the related damage instruction is ignored. [ 359.3.e.5 ] [ 359.3.e.12 ] [ 359.3.f.2.a ]

question: What if my unit's might is reduced before Alpha Strike resolves?
answer: If the friendly unit's might is reduced between finalization and resolution, the total damage pool shrinks accordingly. If the reduced might is now less than the number of chosen enemy unit targets, there is no longer enough damage to assign at least 1 to every target. In that case, you must drop the minimum number of targets such that the number of remaining targets equals the friendly unit's current might [ 355.14.h ] — you cannot drop extra targets to concentrate damage on fewer units. [ 355.14.h.1 ] Any effects triggered by choosing those units as targets remain triggered if the units later cease being targets. [ 355.14.i ] Example You chose 5 enemy units, targeting your friendly unit with 5 might. Before Alpha Strike resolves, your opponent plays a Reaction spell that reduces your unit's might by 2, leaving it at 3 might. You now have only 3 damage to distribute but 5 targets. You must drop 2 targets of your choice. The remaining 3 targets each receive at least 1 of the 3 available damage. You cannot drop extra targets to concentrate damage You chose 3 enemy 1 might Recruits at finalization with a friendly 3 might unit. Before resolution, your opponent reduces your unit's might by 1 with Stupefy (leaving it at 2 might) and buffs one of their Recruits to 2 might with En Garde . You now have 2 damage to distribute but 3 targets. You must drop exactly 1 target — leaving 2 remaining targets that each receive at least 1 damage. You cannot drop 2 targets to leave only the 2 might Recruit and assign both damage to it. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Can I use Arcane Shift to banish my only unit at a battlefield and replay it there?
answer: Yes, as long as you control the battlefield. When Arcane Shift resolves, the replayed unit sits on the chain as a pending item throughout the cleanup that follows. Because a chain exists, the turn is in a closed state, [ 309.1 ] and cleanup step 4 — which would make the battlefield uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [ 323.6 ] The battlefield stays controlled, and when the pending unit is finalized you can choose to replay it there. Attackers cannot replay their unit to the attacking battlefield because they never control it in the first place.

question: Resolution Sequence
answer: When Arcane Shift resolves, the following happens: "Banish a friendly unit" — the unit leaves the board. "then its owner plays it, ignoring its cost" — the unit is added to the chain as a pending item, [ 354.2 ] but its play process pauses while Arcane Shift continues resolving. [ 354.3 ] "Deal 3 to an enemy unit" and "Banish this" both resolve. Arcane Shift finishes resolving, queuing one or more cleanups as outstanding tasks. [ 321.1 ] The cleanups run. The pending unit keeps the chain alive, so the turn remains in a closed state [ 309.1 ] and cleanup step 4 does not apply. [ 323.6 ] Once all outstanding tasks are complete, the pending unit is finalized. [ 334.2 ] You choose where to play it, [ 355.2 ] and the battlefield is still under your control. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Does Astral Heron's ability trigger if it's your first card played to a battlefield this turn?
answer: Yes — assuming it's played to a battlefield. Play, in a trigger condition, refers to a card resolving, not merely being placed on the chain. [ 350.1 ] [ 419.4.a ] Units resolve immediately after they finalize. [ 337.2 ] During that resolution, the unit becomes a game object, its passive abilities become active, and it enters the board at its chosen location. [ 359.2 ] [ 359.2.a ] [ 359.2.c ] A trigger's condition is evaluated after a potentially inciting event has been processed, and nothing requires that event to have been caused by a different card. [ 383.2.c ] [ 383.2.c.1 ] "When you play your first card each turn" begins the trigger condition, [ 383.2.a ] and "if I'm at a battlefield" immediately follows it, so that additional requirement is also part of the trigger condition and is checked when the condition is fulfilled. [ 383.2.a.1 ] After Astral Heron finishes resolving, play-trigger conditions are evaluated. [ 419.4.a ] If it's the first card played this turn, Astral Heron is already at the battlefield when its condition is checked, so its ability is placed on the chain.

question: Does Astral Heron trigger if your first card moves it to base?
answer: No. If a spell such as Flash or Emperor's Divide moves Astral Heron to base while resolving, Astral Heron is no longer at a battlefield when its trigger condition is checked. A card is not considered played, and abilities that trigger from playing it are not evaluated, until that card finishes resolving. [ 350.1 ] [ 419.4.a ] Astral Heron's trigger condition is therefore checked only after the spell's movement instructions have been completed. [ 383.2.c ] Because "if I'm at a battlefield" is part of that trigger condition, the ability is not placed on the chain if Astral Heron is at base by then. [ 383.2.a.1 ] This differs from moving Astral Heron after its triggered ability has already been placed on the chain. At that point, the condition has already been satisfied.

question: Once Astral Heron's triggered ability is on the chain, can killing or moving it stop the cost reduction?
answer: No. Once the triggered ability is on the chain, killing or moving Astral Heron does not stop the discount from applying to your next card. "If I'm at a battlefield" is part of the trigger condition, so it's only checked when the triggering event occurs to decide whether the ability is placed on the chain — it is not re-checked when the ability later resolves. [ 383.2.a.1 ] Nothing in the effect references Astral Heron's location or continued presence, so removing it does not stop the trigger from creating the discount. Once created, that discount is a delayed ability and executes at its specified time regardless of whether Astral Heron remains on the board. [ 392 ]

question: If the spell that receives Astral Heron's discount is later countered, is the discount granted to a different card instead?
answer: No — the discount is spent the moment it reduces that spell's cost. Astral Heron's triggered ability resolves into a delayed passive ability, active only for "your next card" — a single specified window, not a standing effect. [ 390.4 ] [ 391 ] That window belongs to finalizing the next card, not to that card resolving successfully — it doesn't linger to see whether the spell goes on to succeed. Discounts are applied while determining a card's total cost, in step 3 of the play process, and the reduced cost is paid in step 4 — both steps happen well before the card is even finalized, let alone placed on the chain where it could be countered. [ 356.4 ] [ 356.4.a ] [ 357 ] Whichever card is played next consumes that window the moment its cost is reduced; nothing that happens to that card afterward can reopen it. A countered card does nothing and is not considered to have been played, [ 425.1.a ] [ 425.1.b ] and countering does not refund any costs paid to play it, additional costs included. [ 425.1.c ] [ 425.1.c.1 ] That confirms the reduced cost itself stays spent — but Astral Heron's discount was already used up before the spell was even vulnerable to being countered, so there was never anything left to give to a different card. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: If Azir is killed or returned to his base before his attack trigger resolves, do token units still move?
answer: No. "This battlefield" is a referent: information drawn from the source of the ability itself. [ 359.3.f.1 ] Referents are checked at the moment the instruction executes, not when the trigger was placed on the chain. [ 359.3.f.2 ] If Azir has been moved to his base or killed before the trigger resolves, there is no "this battlefield" to move token units to. The instruction cannot be followed and is ignored. [ 359.3.e.6 ] "This battlefield" is not a target. It is programmatically determined from Azir's current location, since he can only ever be at one battlefield at a time — no choice is ever made. [ 355.10.d ] [ 355.10.d.1 ] Two common plays that produce this outcome: Hidden Blade , when played from its facedown zone, can be used in response to Azir's attack trigger to kill him at Reaction speed. Overzealous Fan 's defend trigger fires simultaneously with Azir's attack trigger when combat designations are assigned. Because Azir's controller places their trigger first, Overzealous Fan's trigger sits above it on the chain and resolves first, potentially moving Azir to his base before his own trigger resolves. [ 464.2.e.1 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Can my opponent interact before the friendly unit is killed?
answer: Yes. The friendly unit is selected as a target when the ability is finalized, then killed when the ability resolves. "Kill a friendly unit" comes after the ":" in Baited Hook's activated ability, so it's the first instruction of the effect rather than part of the cost — an activated ability's cost is everything before the ":", and its effect is everything after. [ 377.1 ] Separately, that instruction selects a friendly unit and does not fall under a targeting exception, so the unit is a target chosen and declared during finalization. [ 355.7 ] [ 355.8 ] [ 355.10 ] This is the opposite of cards like Sacrifice , where "kill a friendly unit" is stated as an additional cost and is therefore excluded from targeting entirely. [ 355.10.c ] [ 355.10.c.1 ] After Baited Hook's ability is finalized, opponents have a normal opportunity to play Reactions before it resolves. [ 377.3.b.2 ] [ 406.4 ] Later in the same ability, "up to 1 more than the killed unit" references the unit affected by the earlier "kill" instruction, making the two linked instructions. [ 359.3.e.14 ] Because the unit has already moved to the trash by the time this later instruction checks it, the ability looks back at the unit's characteristics as they were immediately before it changed zones. [ 359.3.e.13 ] Example You activate Baited Hook, targeting a friendly unit with 4 might. In response, your opponent plays Stupefy , reducing that unit's might by 1 down to 3. Stupefy fully resolves before Baited Hook's ability does, so the unit already has 3 might at the moment it's killed. When the ability checks the killed unit's might immediately after, it looks back at that same reduced value — so you may only banish a unit with might up to 4 from among the top 5 cards of your main deck, one lower than if Stupefy hadn't been played.

question: What happens if the targeted unit is removed before Baited Hook's ability resolves?
answer: The unit can't be killed, and no unit can be banished from the top 5, since nothing can satisfy a might comparison against a null value. If the friendly unit is no longer a legal target when the ability resolves — for example, if it was returned to its owner's hand in response — it is unaffected by the ability's "kill" instruction. [ 359.3.e.2 ] [ 359.3.e.5 ] Because the unit was never killed, any information the ability checks about it, including its might, returns null. [ 359.3.e.12 ] "Banish a unit with might up to 1 more than the killed unit" can never be satisfied against a null might, so no unit can be chosen from among the top 5 cards, even though you still look at them. "Then recycle the rest" is unaffected by this, since it isn't tied to the killed unit's might — you still recycle every card you looked at that wasn't banished.

question: If the killed unit has Deathknell, does it resolve before or after the banished unit and its triggers?
answer: After, even though it's finalized first — finalization proceeds in the order items were appended to the chain, but resolution proceeds in the opposite order, newest item first. Baited Hook's ability resolves in its entirety without interruption, [ 354.3 ] so both the killed unit's Deathknell trigger and the unit it later banishes and plays get appended to the chain as pending items during that same resolution, with the Deathknell appended first. Once Baited Hook's ability finishes, those pending items are finalized in that same order — Deathknell first — but the chain then resolves newest-first, so anything appended after the Deathknell , including the played unit's play effect and any abilities triggered by it being played, resolves before it does. The step-by-step below spells this out.

question: Resolution Sequence
answer: Killing Ruined Rex — whose Deathknell reads "Deal 4 to an enemy unit" — as an example: Baited Hook's ability resolves. "Kill a friendly unit" kills Ruined Rex. Ruined Rex's Deathknell trigger is added to the chain as a pending item, on top of Baited Hook's still-resolving ability. [ 428.1.a.1.b ] [ 808.1.d.2 ] Baited Hook's ability continues resolving: you look at the top 5 cards of your main deck and banish a unit with might up to 1 more than Ruined Rex's, then play it ignoring its cost. That unit is added to the chain as a second pending item, above the Deathknell . [ 354.2 ] "Then recycle the rest" executes, and Baited Hook's ability finishes resolving. Two pending items remain: the Deathknell and the banished unit. They must be finalized before anything can resolve, in the order they were appended — the Deathknell first. [ 337.1 ] [ 337.1.b ] Its target — the enemy unit to deal 4 to — is chosen now. [ 355.5 ] The banished unit finalizes next, choosing its location, then resolves immediately by entering the board. [ 337.2 ] If the banished unit has a triggered ability that fires when it's played, that ability is added to the chain now, above the Deathknell , since it was appended later. [ 383.4.a.2 ] [ 340.3 ] Once no pending items remain, the chain resolves top-down: [ 340.4 ] the banished unit's own trigger resolves first, and Ruined Rex's Deathknell — appended before any of this — resolves last, dealing its 4 damage. [ 340.1 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Does Baron Nashor move to the Baron Pit when it's created as part of playing him?
answer: No. Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit directly — his entry location is replaced, not his position on the board. A move is defined as a permanent changing position from one space on the board to another. [ 446.1 ] Baron Nashor is entering the board for the first time (a zone change), which is not a move. [ 446.2 ]

question: What happens after Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit?
answer: A non-combat showdown opens during the resulting cleanup.

question: Resolution Sequence
answer: The Baron Pit is newly created and has no controller when Baron Nashor enters it. [ 439.4.b ] Baron Nashor entering the uncontrolled battlefield applies contested status to it. [ 190.3.a.1 ] During the resulting cleanup, a non-combat showdown is marked as staged at the Baron Pit. [ 316.8.b ] [ 323.8 ] Later in that cleanup, the staged showdown opens. [ 323.12 ] [ 344.2 ] If an opposing unit arrives at the Baron Pit during the showdown, a combat is staged and the non-combat showdown becomes a combat showdown during the following cleanup. [ 316.8.b.1.a ] [ 323.9 ] [ 323.14 ] If the showdown closes with only Baron Nashor's controller's units present at the Baron Pit, and they have not yet scored it this turn, they conquer it and score. [ 348.2.a ] [ 348.2.a.1 ]

question: Does the Baron Pit need to be scored to win by conquering?
answer: Yes. Winning by conquering at match point requires having scored every battlefield on the board that turn — including the Baron Pit. [ 471.1.b.1 ] If it hasn't been scored, the winning conquer draws a card instead. Winning by hold is unaffected, as it has no such requirement. [ 471.1.a.1 ]

question: Can I play Baron Nashor while an opponent's Mageseeker Warden is at a battlefield?
answer: It depends on whether the Baron Pit is already on the board. If the Baron Pit is not yet on the board , Baron Nashor enters the Baron Pit, not your base. As Baron Nashor is played, his "as you play me" instruction fires during the playing process — the Baron Pit battlefield token is added to the board. [ 135.2.b.3 ] [ 187.9 ] Under Mageseeker Warden 's restriction, your base is the only valid playing location — where Baron Nashor is nominally played to — but his replacement effect overrides where he actually enters. [ 355.2.a ] His "If you do, I enter there" then functions as a replacement effect that applies as he enters the board, replacing his entry at his original play location with entry at the Baron Pit. [ 369.3 ] [ 370.1.b ] If the Baron Pit is already on the board , the "as you play me" instruction does nothing — the Baron Pit token is only added if it's not there already — so the "If you do" condition is not met. Baron Nashor simply enters his base, the only valid playing location under Mageseeker Warden's restriction. [ 355.2.a ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Can a unit that's normally untargetable — "can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" — be chosen with Bone Skewer?
answer: Yes, as the untargetability is inactive in hand and hand cards cannot be targeted in any case. Ruin Runner and Baron Nashor are made untargetable by passive abilities declaring that they can't be chosen by some category of spells and abilities. [ 757 ] [ 757.1 ] Passive abilities of permanents are typically active only while on the board. [ 365.1 ] Abilities that function in another zone self-describe that context, [ 366.1 ] which these untargetability abilities do not. They therefore have no effect while the unit is in hand. Beyond that, Bone Skewer never targets the chosen unit in the first place — cards in hand are never targets because the hand is not a public zone, [ 355.10.a ] so there is no finalization step at which a unit there could be declared as a target. [ 355.5 ]

question: Can targeting protection prevent the stun from Bone Skewer?
answer: No, because the reflexive trigger that stuns the unit does not ask its controller to choose anything. If the opponent plays the unit, Bone Skewer's "then do this" wording creates a reflexive trigger as a pending item on the chain. [ 387.1 ] [ 387.2 ] [ 388.1 ] The trigger is linked to the preceding ability, and "it" can only refer to the unit played by that ability. [ 394.1 ] [ 397 ] When the trigger is finalized, no choice is made about which unit will be stunned; it is always and only that unit. Because the unit is programmatically determined rather than chosen, it is not a target. [ 355.10.d ] [ 355.10.d.1 ] This means untargetability — the "can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" passive on units like Ruin Runner and Baron Nashor — does not prevent the stun, since it only stops a unit from being chosen as a target and the stun targets nothing. [ 758 ] Deflect is similarly irrelevant, since Deflect is only added as a cost when a spell or ability chooses an opponent's permanent, [ 809.1.d ] which is not the case here.

question: Can the opponent trigger an optional additional cost effect when playing a unit via Bone Skewer, even though its costs are ignored?
answer: Yes, as declaring the intent to pay is what satisfies the condition, not the amount actually spent. The phrase "any and all costs" in Bone Skewer's text is intentionally broader than the standard "ignoring its cost" wording. Standard cost-ignoring only zeroes out a card's base energy and power costs, [ 356.1.b.1 ] whereas "any and all costs" sets the card's total cost to zero, including non-standard costs like additional costs. [ 356.5.a ] Despite this, the opponent may still declare their intention to pay an optional additional cost during step 2 of playing the card — the decision to pay is made before costs are determined. Once declared, that additional cost is folded into the total cost, which "any and all costs" then sets to zero, so it's already 0 when it comes time to pay. [ 356.5.a ] An optional additional cost is considered paid based on the decision to pay, not the amount actually spent, [ 356.4.f.1 ] so the condition is fully satisfied. Any conditional effect tied to "if you paid the additional cost" therefore triggers normally. Example You play Bone Skewer and choose Nami, Headstrong from your opponent's hand. Your opponent is instructed to play Nami to the chosen battlefield, ignoring any and all costs. As part of that process, they declare their intention to pay the optional additional cost of . That cost is already 0, so nothing is actually paid — but because they chose to pay it, the condition is met. Nami's triggered ability fires, stunning an enemy unit. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Can I choose a unit's current battlefield as Call to Battle's destination?
answer: No, because Call to Battle requires the player to choose the move destination, so the restriction on valid destinations applies directly. When a spell or ability has the player choose a move destination, that destination must be somewhere other than the unit's current location. [ 355.4 ] [ 355.4.a ] Call to Battle has the player choose both the unit and the battlefield, so the chosen battlefield cannot be the unit's current location. If no valid destination can be chosen for the selected unit, the spell cannot be finalized. This contrasts with Flash , which specifies its destination — base — rather than requiring the player to choose one. Because no destination choice is made when playing Flash, this restriction never applies, and a unit already in base is a valid target. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: When I play Consuming Curse from my trash, does it count itself for the bonus damage?
answer: No. Playing Consuming Curse from your trash moves it onto the chain first, [ 354 ] [ 419.1 ] so it's no longer in your trash to be counted. Only the other copies still in your trash add bonus damage. Shadow Assassin and Shadowblade Lurker work the same way. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: When does Diana's ability trigger relative to attack and defend triggers?
answer: Diana's ability resolves after all attack and defend triggers generated as that combat opens. When combat opens with a combat showdown, the attacker and defender designations are assigned to units. [ 464.2.c.3 ] Attack triggers fire when a unit gains the attacker designation, and defend triggers fire when a unit gains the defender designation. [ 383.4.e ] [ 383.4.f ] Those triggers are then added to the combat chain, with the attacking player placing theirs first, followed by others in turn order, and the defending player last. [ 464.2.e ] [ 464.2.e.1 ] Diana's "when a showdown begins here" trigger is a start-of-showdown effect, which the combat-opening sequence processes as its very first step — before designations are established and their attack and defend triggers are added to the chain. [ 464.2.b ] Because the chain resolves newest-item-first, Diana's ability resolves last — after every attack and defend trigger from that same combat chain has already resolved. [ 340.1 ]

question: How does Diana's ability work?
answer: When a showdown begins at Diana's battlefield, you may pay 1 to finalize her triggered ability onto the chain. Outdated CR example Diana received a functional errata alongside the Core Rules 1.4 update. Older printings say "you may pay 1 . If you do, ..."; her updated text says "you may pay 1 to ..." instead. This changes the energy payment from an instruction performed during resolution into a cost paid while finalizing the ability. CR 444.2 still describes Diana using her pre-errata behavior and incorrectly places the payment on resolution. [ 444.2 ] Because "you may" is the first part of the effect, you choose whether to perform the ability during finalization. [ 383.3.a ] The immediately following "pay 1 to Predict " is a cost within instructions, so the payment is treated as the triggered ability's base cost and must be paid for the ability to finalize. [ 383.3.b ] [ 383.3.b.1 ] You may activate Add reactions while paying this cost. [ 444.2.c ] If you do not pay, the ability does not finalize and none of its effects occur. If you pay, the ability is placed on the chain; when it resolves, you Predict , reveal the top card of your main deck, and draw that card if it is a spell. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: How does Emperor's Dais's ability work?
answer: When you conquer Emperor's Dais, you may pay 1 and return a unit you control there to its owner's hand to finalize the triggered ability onto the chain. Core Rules 1.4 errata Emperor's Dais received a functional errata alongside the Core Rules 1.4 update. Older printings separate "pay 1 and return a unit" from "If you do, play a 2 Might Sand Soldier unit token"; its updated text joins them using "to" instead. This makes the energy payment and unit return parts of a single cost performed while finalizing the ability, so the unit can no longer be returned without also paying the energy. Because "you may" is the first part of the effect, you choose whether to perform the ability during finalization. [ 383.3.a ] The immediately following "pay 1 and return a unit ... to play" is a cost within instructions, so both actions form the triggered ability's base cost and must be completed for the ability to finalize. [ 383.3.b ] [ 383.3.b.1 ] [ 404.1 ] You may activate Add reactions while paying the energy portion of this cost. [ 444.2.c ] Returning the unit is part of the cost, so that unit is not a target and returns to its owner's hand during finalization rather than resolution. [ 355.10.c.1 ] If you cannot or choose not to pay the entire cost, the ability does not finalize; you cannot return the unit without also paying the energy. [ 404.2 ] If you complete the cost, the ability is placed on the chain; when it resolves, you play a 2 Might Sand Soldier unit token at Emperor's Dais. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: What are "optional additional costs"?
answer: Optional additional costs are costs that: [ 356.2.b.1 ] Use the exact phrase "as an additional cost" Include the word "may" Ezreal, Prodigy's passive ability reads "Optional additional costs you pay cost 1 or less." It only reduces costs that meet both criteria. Accelerate and Repeat are keyworded instances of optional additional costs, [ 805.1.a ] [ 820.1.d ] so they are also reduced by Ezreal's ability. Optional additional costs are determined when you calculate a card's total cost during the playing process, and Ezreal's discount is applied when you apply discounts. [ 356.4 ] Ezreal's discount is a component discount — it applies to a specific component of the cost (the optional additional cost) rather than to the total cost, so it is applied as soon as that component is added, before any general cost discounts take effect. [ 356.4.c ] Example Blast Corps Cadet 's ability reads "You may pay 1 as an additional cost to play me." This is an optional additional cost because it uses both "as an additional cost" and "may." Ezreal's ability would reduce this cost to 1 or . Example You play Sivir, Mercenary with Accelerate 1 while you control Ezreal, Prodigy. With Ezreal's ability, you can choose to reduce this to either 1 or .

question: What doesn't count as an optional additional cost?
answer: Several similar-looking costs are not optional additional costs and are not reduced by Ezreal's ability.

question: Mandatory additional costs
answer: Example Cruel Patron reads "As an additional cost to play me, kill a friendly unit." This is not an optional additional cost: it uses "as an additional cost" but not "may," making it a mandatory additional cost. [ 356.2.a.1 ]

question: Costs in effects
answer: Example Hard Bargain 's effect reads "Counter a spell unless its controller pays 2 ." The controller's 2 payment is not an optional additional cost. It appears inside Hard Bargain's effect rather than being paid to play the spell, so Ezreal does not reduce it. Hard Bargain's separate Repeat cost is an optional additional cost and is reduced by Ezreal. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Can Flash target a unit that is already in base?
answer: Yes, because Flash specifies its destination rather than requiring the player to choose one. When a spell or ability has the player choose a move destination, that destination must be somewhere other than the unit's current location. [ 355.4 ] [ 355.4.a ] Flash, however, does not ask the player to choose a destination: the card specifies it as base. That step of the play process never occurs, so this restriction never applies. The only choice the player makes when playing Flash is which friendly units to target. [ 355.5 ] A unit in base is a friendly unit and meets no other targeting restriction, so it is a valid target. [ 355.9.b ] When Flash resolves and instructs the game to move that unit to base, the instruction is impossible — a unit cannot move to its current location. Impossible instructions are ignored, and everything else resolves normally. [ 055 ] Azir, Ascendant illustrates the same principle: its ability says "Move me to its location and it to my original location," where both destinations are derived from the game state rather than chosen by the player. Choosing a unit at Azir's current location is legal; the impossible swap is ignored at resolution. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Does Gangplank's replacement effect stop the rest of a spell or ability from resolving?
answer: No. A replacement effect only replaces the specific event or instruction that qualifies for it. [ 370.1 ] For Gangplank, that means a stun, might decrease, or return to hand caused by a spell or ability that chose him. Example A player plays Star-Crossed , targeting their own Empowered Gangplank as the friendly unit and an opponent's Elder Dragon as the enemy unit. Returning Elder Dragon doesn't choose Gangplank, so his replacement effect has nothing to apply to there — it's returned to hand as normal. Returning Gangplank is the qualifying event: instead of going to hand, he gets +3 might. The rest of Star-Crossed resolves normally; it simply produces a different result for the one instruction that involves Gangplank.

question: How does Gangplank's replacement effect interact with Switcheroo?
answer: Only the modifier applied to Gangplank is a candidate for replacement — whatever happens to the other unit is untouched. See How does Switcheroo work? for why swapping creates two separate modifiers from a single calculated difference. [ 433.1.a ] [ 433.1.b ] Switcheroo chooses Gangplank when the spell is finalized, then creates one modifier for each unit when it resolves. If the modifier affecting Gangplank would decrease his might, that event is replaced with +3 might because it comes from a spell that chose him. If it would increase his might, it does not match the events his ability replaces and applies normally. The modifier affecting the other unit is unchanged, and the difference is not recalculated. Example An Empowered Gangplank at 6 might is swapped with a 1 might Determined Sentry at the same battlefield via Switcheroo . The swap action calculates a difference of 5, then creates two modifiers: -5 might for Gangplank and +5 might for Determined Sentry. Gangplank's replacement effect intercedes on his -5 might modifier — decreasing his might is one of the events it replaces — and turns it into +3 might instead. The +5 might modifier applies only to Determined Sentry, so Gangplank's replacement effect does not affect it. Gangplank ends at 9 might (6 base + 3); Determined Sentry ends at 6 might (1 base + 5). How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Can Glasc Mixologist's Deathknell target a unit that died from the same event?
answer: Yes, because targets are not chosen until the ability is finalized — by which point all units that died in the same event are already in the trash. Whenever a unit with Deathknell dies, its trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item. [ 808.1.d.2 ] During a cleanup, this ordering is enforced system-wide: step 3a queues all Deathknell triggers from every unit with lethal damage [ 323.4 ] and only then does step 3b move those units to the trash. [ 323.5 ] The same result applies when one kill instruction kills multiple units. Their deaths are simultaneous because they result from the same game action, [ 370.1.a.2 ] and each relevant Deathknell becomes pending before its unit moves to the trash. [ 428.1.a.1.b ] [ 808.1.d.2 ] In either case, all units that died from that event are in the trash before the pending ability is finalized and its target is chosen. [ 334.2 ] [ 355.8 ]

question: Can Glasc Mixologist's Deathknell play a unit to the battlefield where he died?
answer: Yes, as long as you controlled that battlefield when Glasc Mixologist died. Outside a showdown , the Deathknell trigger remains on the chain as a pending item from the moment it is queued. Because a chain exists, the turn remains in a closed state, [ 309.1 ] and cleanup step 4 — which makes unoccupied battlefields uncontrolled — only applies during an open state. [ 323.6 ] The battlefield stays under your control, so when the unit is finalized you can choose it as a valid destination. [ 355.2.a ] During a showdown , control of the battlefield cannot change until instructed by the steps of the combat or showdown, [ 190.4.b ] so the question does not arise.

question: What happens when Glasc Mixologist is my only defender and his Deathknell plays a unit where he died?
answer: Several things here commonly catch players off guard: surviving enemy units heal to full before the new unit arrives, neither player wins the original combat, and a second combat immediately follows. The combat cleanup heals all units before any pending trigger can resolve, [ 466.1.a.1 ] [ 334 ] so by the time Glasc's Deathknell finalizes and the new unit reaches the battlefield, the enemy is already back to full health. Because Glasc was your only defender, no defenders remain during cleanup step 3d, so the surviving attackers are not recalled. [ 466.1.a.2 ] With units from both players now present, combat result is determined. Because both players have units there, the result is "No Result." [ 466.3.d ] A fresh combat is immediately staged at that battlefield. [ 466.3.d.1 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: If Heedless Resurrection is countered, is the killed unit returned?
answer: No, as the kill is an additional cost and countering a spell never refunds costs already paid. Killing a friendly unit is an additional cost required to play Heedless Resurrection. A countered spell does nothing and is cleared from the chain. [ 425.1.a ] Countering does not refund any costs paid to play a card, including additional costs. [ 425.1.c ] [ 425.1.c.1 ] That cost is paid before the spell resolves, so the killed unit is not returned.

question: Can I kill a unit with Heedless Resurrection's cost and then resurrect that same unit?
answer: No, as the resurrection target must already be in your trash when you choose it, before the kill cost is paid. When playing Heedless Resurrection, you must choose the unit to resurrect during step 2 of finalization — the "Make relevant choices" step. [ 355.5 ] At that point, the unit you intend to kill is still on the board, not yet in your trash. "A unit from your trash" must be in your trash to be a valid target, [ 355.9.a ] so a living unit on the board cannot be chosen. The additional cost — killing a friendly unit — is paid in step 4, [ 357.2 ] after all choices are already locked in. [ 355.15 ]

question: Does "ignoring its cost" when resurrecting a unit also ignore that unit's additional costs, such as Accelerate?
answer: No. "Ignoring its cost" only sets the resurrected unit's base energy and power costs to zero; additional costs are not waived. When Heedless Resurrection instructs you to play a unit from your trash "ignoring its cost," that instruction sets the resurrected unit's base energy cost and base power cost to zero. [ 356.1.b.1 ] Additional costs — such as the optional Accelerate cost — are applied in a separate step after the base cost is zeroed out and are unaffected by the "ignoring its cost" instruction. [ 356.1.b.3 ] If the resurrected unit has an optional additional cost you may choose whether to pay it; [ 356.2.b.1 ] if it has a mandatory additional cost you must pay it. [ 356.2.a.1 ]

question: If Heedless Resurrection gains Repeat, do I need to kill a friendly unit for each repetition?
answer: No. The additional cost to kill a friendly unit is paid once, as part of playing the spell. Additional costs like this are paid during step 4 of playing the card, [ 357.2 ] not during resolution. Repeat makes the spell's instructions execute an additional time upon resolution, [ 820.1.d.1 ] but does not re-run costs that were already paid while playing — "as you play me" instructions execute once, before the Repeat execution ever occurs. [ 135.2.b.3 ] No matter how many times Repeat is paid, the spell is only played once, [ 820.3.a ] so you kill only one friendly unit. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Does the target's controller draw if the kill is replaced?
answer: Yes. Replacing Hidden Blade's kill does not prevent its linked draw instruction from executing. The phrase "its controller" links the draw to the unit affected by the preceding kill instruction. [ 359.3.e.14 ] Replacing that kill action does not stop the later linked instruction unless it directly references the action itself. [ 359.3.e.14.b ] Hidden Blade's draw references the targeted unit's controller, not whether the unit was killed, so the draw still executes. Example You play Hidden Blade targeting an opponent's unit. They respond with Zhonya's Hourglass , which replaces the unit's death. The unit is not killed. Because it was still a legal target when Hidden Blade resolved, the opponent draws 2.

question: Does the controller draw if the target becomes illegal?
answer: No. An illegal target is entirely unaffected by the spell, and the draw is no exception. An illegal target is unaffected by the spell, so Hidden Blade's kill instruction is ignored. [ 359.3.e.5 ] When an earlier linked instruction is ignored, its later linked instructions are also ignored, so the controller does not draw. [ 359.3.e.14.a ] Example You play Hidden Blade targeting an opponent's unit at a battlefield. They respond by moving it to their base using Flash . Hidden Blade resolves. The unit is no longer at a battlefield, so it is an illegal target. The unit is not killed and the opponent does not draw. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: If I target Irelia with a spell or ability and it gets countered, does she still get +1 might?
answer: Yes. Irelia is chosen as a target during step 2 of playing the spell or ability — the "Make relevant choices" step. [ 355.5 ] [ 355.7 ] This happens before the spell or ability is finalized on the chain and before opponents have any opportunity to react. After the spell or ability finishes finalizing, her targeting effect is added to the chain as a pending item. [ 383.4.b.2 ] [ 383.4.b.3 ] That trigger is finalized before opponents receive an opportunity to react. [ 337.3 ] [ 337.4 ] The trigger is not contingent on the spell or ability that caused it successfully resolving. Countering the spell or ability only prevents it from resolving [ 425.1.a ] — it has no bearing on Irelia's already-triggered ability. Blade Dancer works the same way. Her triggered ability reads "When you choose a friendly unit, you may exhaust me and pay to ready it." It ends up on the chain before the original spell can be countered.

question: Does Blade Dancer's ability trigger Irelia's +1 might?
answer: Not from choosing — but she can still trigger from being readied if she was exhausted. Blade Dancer does not choose a unit — it does not target. [ 355.10.d ] [ 355.10.d.1 ] "It" in "ready it" deterministically refers back to the unit already identified as Blade Dancer's trigger condition, with no separate choice made by the player. Irelia's ability can only trigger from Blade Dancer if she was exhausted and is readied by it — and only through the readying half of her ability, not the choosing half. [ 415.1 ]

question: Does Irelia get +1 might when she readies during the Awaken Phase?
answer: Yes, but only if she was exhausted and actually transitions to the ready state. During the Awaken Phase at the start of each turn, the turn player readies all game objects they control that are able to be readied. [ 315.1.b ] Readying is the action of marking a game object as available for action. [ 415.1 ] If Irelia was exhausted, she transitions to ready and her trigger fires. If she is already ready at the start of your turn, she cannot be readied again [ 415.1.b ] — no readying event occurs and the trigger does not fire.

question: Does a Repeat spell targeting Irelia for both instructions give her +1 might twice?
answer: Yes, as choosing her for each instruction is a separate triggering event. Repeat is functionally "execute the spell's instructions one additional time". [ 820.1.d ] When the Repeat cost is paid, choices for both executions are made during the same "Make relevant choices" step of playing the card. [ 820.2 ] [ 820.2.a ] Choosing Irelia for the first instruction and choosing her for the second target her twice. After the spell finalizes, her targeting effect is added to the chain as a pending item once for each targeting event. [ 383.4.b.2 ] [ 383.4.b.3 ] Example You play Feral Strength and pay its Repeat cost, choosing Irelia for both instructions. After Feral Strength finalizes, Irelia's ability triggers twice — once per targeting event — and both triggers are added to the chain. When her triggers resolve, she receives +1 and +1 from her own ability. When the spell resolves, Irelia receives +2 and +2 from the spell's two instructions. That's +6 might total this turn. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: If I move Irresistible Faefolk to an open battlefield and pull an enemy unit there, who is the attacker?
answer: You — the Irresistible Faefolk player — are the attacker. When Irresistible Faefolk moves to an open (uncontrolled) battlefield, that move applies the contested status to the battlefield. [ 450 ] [ 190.3.a ] Irresistible Faefolk's trigger resolves after the cleanup caused by its own move, moving the enemy unit to that battlefield. During the cleanup following the enemy unit's move, combat is staged because opposing units are now present at the contested battlefield. [ 319.8 ] [ 323.9 ] When combat opens, the attacker is defined as the player whose unit(s) applied the contested status. [ 464.2.c.1 ] That is you — the player who moved Irresistible Faefolk. The opponent whose unit was pulled in is the defender. [ 464.2.c.2 ]

question: If I play Irresistible Faefolk directly to a battlefield, does its ability trigger?
answer: No — playing a unit to a battlefield is not a move, so the ability does not trigger. A move is defined as a permanent changing its position from one location on the board to another. [ 446.1 ] Playing a card involves it entering the board from a non-board zone (such as your hand), which is a zone change, not a move. [ 446.2 ] Because Irresistible Faefolk's ability specifically triggers when it moves to a battlefield, playing it directly there does not satisfy that trigger condition.

question: If an opponent responds to my move trigger by removing Irresistible Faefolk from the battlefield, does the enemy unit still move?
answer: Yes — the enemy unit still moves to that battlefield. Irresistible Faefolk's trigger condition is moving to a battlefield, and "that battlefield" in the effect is a referent to the battlefield named in that trigger condition. Information referenced from a trigger condition is checked when the trigger condition is fulfilled, not when the ability resolves. [ 359.3.f.3 ] That means "that battlefield" was already fixed the moment Irresistible Faefolk moved there and placed the ability on the chain. Suppose an opponent responds to the triggered ability by playing Gust (or similarly, Star-Crossed ), targeting Irresistible Faefolk itself to return it to your hand. Irresistible Faefolk returns to your hand, but the triggered ability is unaffected — it's already an independent item on the chain, and the battlefield it references was fixed at trigger time. When it resolves, it moves an enemy unit to that battlefield, even though Irresistible Faefolk is no longer there. This differs from information derived from an ability's source or targets, which is generally checked when the referencing instruction executes and may become unavailable before resolution. [ 359.3.f.1 ] [ 359.3.f.2 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Does Karthus's ability apply if he dies from the same effect as the unit with Deathknell?
answer: Yes, because Deathknell triggers are always queued as pending items before the dying unit leaves the board. Whenever a unit with Deathknell is killed — whether by a kill effect or by lethal damage during cleanup — its trigger is added to the chain before the card is moved to the trash. [ 808.1.d.2 ] Karthus's passive is only active while he is on the board. [ 365.1 ] When one kill action kills Karthus and another unit simultaneously, as with The Ruination , Karthus is still present when that unit's Deathknell triggers. [ 370.1.a.2 ] In the cleanup case this ordering is enforced explicitly: step 3a queues all Deathknell triggers [ 323.4 ] before step 3b moves any of those units to the trash. [ 323.5 ] Example You control Karthus and a friendly unit with Deathknell . Your opponent plays The Ruination , which kills all units. Both are sent to the trash, but not before Karthus's ability doubles the Deathknell trigger.

question: Does a single Not So Fast counter both Deathknell triggers when Karthus is on the board?
answer: No. If both Deathknell triggers are legal targets for Not So Fast , one copy can counter only one of them. When a friendly unit with Deathknell dies while Karthus is on the board, his ability causes that Deathknell to trigger an additional time. Each trigger is added to the chain as its own independent pending item. [ 808.1.d.2 ] Not So Fast targets a single spell or ability, so each copy can counter only one trigger. This applies only when the Deathknell ability chooses one of your friendly units or gear. Otherwise, Not So Fast cannot target either trigger. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Can an opponent play a unit in reaction to Kha'Zix's trigger to prevent the effect?
answer: No. Once Kha'Zix's ability is on the chain, adding more units cannot prevent it from resolving. Kha'Zix's ability reads "When I attack or defend, if an enemy unit is alone here, give me +2 Might this turn and gain 2 XP." The "if" clause immediately follows the initial trigger clause, so it is part of the trigger condition. [ 383.2.a.1 ] The condition is evaluated once, when Kha'Zix gains the attacker or defender designation. [ 383.4.e.2.b ] [ 383.4.f.2.b ] If the enemy unit is alone then, the ability is placed on the chain and a later arrival cannot undo it. If the enemy unit is not alone then, the ability does not trigger even if another enemy unit is later removed. Contrast: if the condition were at the end If Kha'Zix instead read "When I attack or defend, give me +2 Might this turn and gain 2 XP if an enemy unit is alone here," the "if" clause would come after the effect instruction rather than immediately after the trigger condition. In that case the "if" would be part of the effect rather than the trigger condition: the ability would go on the chain whenever Kha'Zix attacks or defends, regardless of whether an enemy unit is alone, and the condition would only be evaluated when it resolves. An opponent could then play a unit at reaction speed to ensure two units are present at resolution, preventing the +2 Might and the 2 XP.

question: Can Kha'Zix trigger multiple times in the same turn?
answer: Yes. The once-per-combat limit on attack and defend triggers applies to each combat individually, not to the entire turn, so Kha'Zix can gain +2 might and 2 XP once in each separate combat it participates in. [ 383.4.e.2.a ] [ 383.4.f.2.a ] Each time Kha'Zix enters a new combat it gains its attacker or defender designation for the first time in that combat, which is what triggers the ability. There is no rule preventing a unit from participating in multiple combats per turn, and each combat is an independent instance with its own once-per-combat tracking. Example After Kha'Zix wins a combat and the state returns to neutral open, you can play Charm to pull a different enemy unit onto Kha'Zix's battlefield. That unit becoming present at a battlefield Kha'Zix's controller already controls applies contested status, staging a new, distinct combat. When that combat opens, Kha'Zix gains the defender designation for the first time in that combat. If the pulled unit is alone, the additional requirement in the trigger condition is satisfied and Kha'Zix triggers again. Playing additional Charms repeats this cycle for as long as enemy units and Charms are available. For more on how attack and defend triggers work per combat, see When do attack/defend triggers happen? . How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Can Lacerate target a unit that doesn't have 3 might or less?
answer: Yes, Lacerate can target any otherwise legal unit, regardless of its might. "Choose a unit" targets a unit, [ 355.7 ] [ 355.9.a ] and adds no might-based targeting restriction — "unit" only identifies the category of game object being targeted. [ 355.9.a.1 ] The instruction to kill it "if it has 3 might or less" is not part of the target description at all — it's a condition checked on the effect itself as Lacerate resolves. This is unlike a card such as Gust , which reads "Return a unit at a battlefield with 3 might or less to its owner's hand" — there, "with 3 might or less" describes the target, so it's a genuine targeting restriction and only such units are valid choices. [ 355.9.b ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: If my opponent targets my spell with Lilting Lullaby and I counter my own spell in response, can I still play spells?
answer: Yes. Countering your own spell removes it from the chain, so Lilting Lullaby has no valid target when it resolves — and with nothing to counter, the linked restriction on playing spells is also ignored. When you counter your own spell, it is cleared from the chain. [ 425.1.a ] "Spell" in a targeting context refers to objects on the chain. [ 355.9.a.2 ] By the time Lilting Lullaby resolves, its target is no longer on the chain and no longer meets the targeting requirements — this is mistargeting. [ 359.3.e.2 ] [ 359.3.e.9 ] Because all of Lilting Lullaby's first instruction's targets are now invalid, the "Counter a spell" instruction does not execute. [ 359.3.e.7 ] "Counter a spell" and "Its controller can't play spells this turn" are linked instructions — the second references the controller of the spell from the first. Since the earlier linked instruction was ignored, the later one is ignored as well. [ 359.3.e.14.a ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: Does Lotus Trap affect how much damage needs to be assigned in combat?
answer: Yes. When damage is assigned in the combat damage step, a replacement effect that would apply to the resulting damage is considered to apply to the assignment instead, so Lotus Trap's doubling takes effect as damage is assigned — not only when it is dealt. Assigning damage and dealing damage are still distinct steps. [ 465.2.c.1 ] [ 465.2.c.1.a ] But the rules fold damage replacement effects into the assignment step: any replacement effect that would apply to the resulting damage is applied to the assignment. [ 465.2.c.5 ] A unit must have lethal damage assigned to it in full before any remaining damage may be assigned elsewhere, [ 465.2.c.3 ] so the doubling changes how much of the attacker's damage the unit ties up. The assigning player picks the smallest raw amount that, once doubled, reaches lethal damage — for a 3 might unit under Lotus Trap, assigning 2 raw damage doubles to 4, so only 2 need be committed to kill it. [ 465.2.c.4.a ] When damage is finally dealt it is not doubled again, since the doubling already happened during assignment. [ 465.2.d ] If more than one replacement effect applies to the unit — for example a prevent effect alongside Lotus Trap — the unit's controller chooses the order they apply during assignment, which can change the final assigned and dealt amounts. [ 465.2.c.5 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Does Nocturne's ability apply when Burn or Minefield puts it into the trash?
answer: No. Neither Burn nor Minefield instructs you to look at or reveal Nocturne. Rules citation needed "Look" is not yet defined as its own numbered action the way "reveal" is. The core rules consistently treat it as a parallel, explicitly-instructed action alongside reveal wherever both are mentioned, and this ruling relies on that pattern — an official update giving "look" its own definition would let this be cited directly. Nocturne's ability reads "As you look at or reveal me from the top of your deck, you may banish me. If you do, you may play me for ." The word "as" identifies this as a replacement effect that can apply only while the qualifying look or reveal event is being processed. question: How does Smite interact with death-saving replacement effects?

question: How does Switcheroo work?
answer: Switcheroo does not swap might values directly — it determines the difference in current might at resolution and applies +X/-X modifiers accordingly. Switcheroo uses the Swap action, [ 433 ] which calculates the difference between the two units' current might, then applies a -X modifier to the higher might unit and a +X modifier to the lower might unit. Current might means the unit's total might at resolution time, including all active modifiers: equipment bonuses, battlefield passives, conditional abilities, and any other effects. The modifiers Switcheroo applies persist until end of turn.

question: Are existing equipment bonuses or passive effects counted again after Switcheroo resolves?
answer: No. Equipment bonuses, battlefield passives, and conditional abilities are already factored into current might when Switcheroo resolves. New modifiers that begin applying after Switcheroo resolves still apply normally, but they do not change the modifiers Switcheroo already created. Example You have a unit with 2 base might and attached equipment granting +3 might, giving it 5 current might. Your opponent has a 1 might unit at the same battlefield. When Switcheroo resolves, it calculates a difference of 4 and applies -4 to your unit and +4 to your opponent's. Your unit ends up at 1 might; your opponent's at 5. The equipment bonus was already included in the calculation — you cannot reapply the +3 afterwards.

question: What happens when equipment detaches or passives stop applying after Switcheroo?
answer: The Switcheroo modifier persists until end of turn, but the equipment or passive bonus is removed independently — which can result in very low or negative might. Each modifier is independent: when equipment detaches or a passive deactivates, only that specific bonus is removed; the Switcheroo modifier remains until end of turn.

question: Equipment detaching
answer: Example Your unit has 2 base might and +3 from attached equipment (5 current might total). After swapping with a 1 might unit, Switcheroo applies -4 to your unit, leaving it at 1 might (2 base - 4 from Switcheroo + 3 from equipment). If the equipment later detaches, your unit loses the +3 bonus but keeps the -4 from Switcheroo, leaving it at -2 might.

question: Passives
answer: Example Trifarian War Camp grants units +1 might while they're present. Your 1 might unit (currently 2 with the battlefield bonus) swaps with your opponent's 6 might unit at the same battlefield. Switcheroo applies +4 to your unit and -4 to your opponent's, leaving your unit at 6 might (1 base + 4 from Switcheroo + 1 from War Camp). If it later moves away from War Camp, it loses the +1 and drops to 5 might — the +4 from Switcheroo stays until end of turn. Example Wuju Bladesman grants a friendly unit +2 might while it defends alone. Your 3 might unit is defending alone, making its current might 5 with Wuju's bonus, while your opponent's attacking unit has 1 might. Your opponent plays Switcheroo targeting both units. Switcheroo applies -4 to your defender and +4 to the attacker, leaving your defender at 1 might (3 base - 4 from Switcheroo + 2 from Wuju) and the attacker at 5 might (1 base + 4 from Switcheroo). Once Wuju's passive deactivates — when combat ends or another friendly unit joins the defense — your unit drops to -1 might.

question: Can Switcheroo result in negative might?
answer: Yes. When referenced by spells or abilities and when summing combat damage, negative might is treated as 0, but might increases and decreases use the actual negative value. Units can end up with negative might when modifiers included in their current might at resolution are later removed. Units with might less than 0 are treated as having 0 might when referenced by spells and abilities, and when summing might to be assigned as damage in the Combat Damage Step. [ 143.2.b ] Units with 0 or negative might do not automatically die — units are only killed during cleanup if they have lethal damage, meaning non-zero damage equal to or exceeding their might. [ 323.5 ] [ 142.4.b ] If a unit later gains additional might modifiers, they add to the actual negative value. Example A unit at -2 might is targeted with Punch First , which reads "Give a unit +5 Might this turn." The unit ends up with 3 might — the +5 modifier adds to the actual -2 value. How was this page? question: Can Temporal Breach banish a unit at a different battlefield if played from Hidden?

[ 811.1.d.2 ] Temporal Breach's own wording doesn't restrict its target to a location, so this Hidden restriction applies in full — a unit at another battlefield, or in base, isn't a legal target when it's played from Hidden. If Temporal Breach is played normally, the Hidden restriction does not apply. It may target an otherwise legal unit at any board location, including a base or battlefield. [ 811.3 ]

question: Can I banish my only unit at a battlefield I control and replay it there without losing control in between?

[ 323.6 ] Control is never lost, so any effects that care about gaining or losing control of that battlefield don't trigger. When all outstanding tasks are complete, the pending unit is finalized [ 334.2 ] [ 337.1 ] and replayed to the same battlefield you still control, as dictated by Temporal Breach's own text. question: When do triggered abilities trigger?
answer: When their condition is met, triggered abilities are added to the chain as pending items, regardless of whose turn it is. [ 383.3 ] [ 383.3.c ] The Reaction keyword is not required for this to work on an opponent's turn. Unlike spells and activated abilities which require Reaction to be played outside your turn, satisfying a trigger condition automatically creates the pending ability. That ability must still finalize: it may be removed if its controller declines an initial "you may," if legal choices are unavailable, or if a required trigger cost is not paid. [ 383.3.a.2 ] [ 402.4 ] [ 404.2 ] Example Blade Dancer triggers when you choose a friendly unit. This can happen on your opponent's turn, for example when you play a Reaction spell that targets one of your own units.

question: Can I react to triggered and activated abilities?
answer: Yes, with one important exception: abilities that use the Add keyword. All triggered and activated abilities are placed on the chain. [ 377.3 ] [ 383.3 ] However, abilities that add resources resolve immediately when finalized, which means players do not receive priority to react to them. [ 337.2 ] [ 429.2 ] [ 429.2.a ]

question: How are additional conditions in triggered abilities evaluated?
answer: It depends on where the condition appears in the ability's text. The trigger condition begins with "When," "At," or "The [Nth] time" and includes the event and any qualifiers attached to it. [ 383.2.a ] An additional conditional statement immediately following that condition is also part of the trigger condition, even if it appears after a comma. [ 383.2.a.1 ] The remaining instructions form the ability's effect. [ 383.2.b ] Every requirement in the trigger condition must be satisfied for the ability to be placed on the chain. For example, Sunken Temple reads "When you conquer here with one or more Mighty units, you may pay 1 to draw 1." The requirement that the conquering units be Mighty is embedded in the trigger condition; if no Mighty unit participated in the conquer, the ability does not trigger. An "if" clause that immediately follows the trigger condition is therefore part of that condition and checked when the triggering event occurs. If the condition is not satisfied at the moment the triggering event occurs, the ability is never placed on the chain at all. [ 383.2.a.1 ] However, "if" clauses embedded within the effect text — coming after an effect instruction rather than immediately following the trigger condition — are only checked on resolution. The ability goes on the chain regardless, and the condition is only evaluated when it resolves. Example Gutter Palace reads "At the start of your Beginning Phase, if you have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields, you win the game." The "if" clause immediately follows the trigger condition, so it is part of that condition and checked when the triggering event occurs. This ability is only placed on the chain if you already have exactly 4 cards in hand and exactly 4 units at battlefields at the start of your Beginning Phase. If the condition is not satisfied at that moment, the ability does not trigger at all. Example Loose Cannon reads "At start of your Beginning Phase, draw 1 if you have one or fewer cards in your hand." Here the "if" clause does not immediately follow the trigger condition — it comes after the effect instruction "draw 1". This means it is part of the effect and is checked on resolution. The ability goes on the chain at the start of every one of your Beginning Phases, regardless of how many cards are in your hand. Only when the ability resolves is the hand size checked; if you have more than one card at that point, the draw does not happen.

question: When do I decide whether to perform a triggered ability that says "you may"?
answer: It depends on where "you may" appears in the ability's effect. If "you may" is the first part of the effect, you decide whether to perform the ability during finalization. [ 383.3.a ] [ 402.1 ] If you decline, the pending ability is removed from the chain and considered not to have triggered. [ 383.3.a.2 ] [ 402.1.a ] If you accept, you make all choices required for finalization and pay any costs incurred during finalization before the ability can finalize. [ 402.2 ] [ 404 ] If "you may" appears later in the effect, you decide whether to perform that instruction when the ability resolves. [ 383.3.a.3 ]

question: When do I pay costs within instructions using "may"?
answer: It depends on where the cost appears in the triggered ability's effect. In rules text phrased as "[do X] to [do Y]," the [do X] part is considered a cost within instructions. If that cost appears at the beginning of a triggered effect or immediately after an initial "you may," it becomes the ability's base cost and must be paid during finalization. [ 383.3.b ] [ 383.3.b.1 ] [ 740.4.a.2 ] [ 403.1.b.1 ] If you decline to pay, the pending ability is removed from the chain without finalizing. [ 404.2 ] If the cost appears later in the triggered effect, you pay it when the ability resolves. [ 740.4.a.2.a ] Example Vayne, Hunter 's ability reads "When I conquer, you may pay 1 to return me to my owner's hand." It will trigger when you conquer. At finalization, you must decide whether to pay the 1 cost. If you decline, the pending ability is removed from the chain. If you pay, the ability finalizes and opponents have the opportunity to react before it resolves. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Can I react to units being played?
answer: No, as units enter the board immediately without priority being passed to other players. Unlike spells, units resolve the moment they are finalized and do not open a window of opportunity for reactions. [ 337.2 ] [ 359.2 ] If the unit has a play effect ("When you play me…"), or if another permanent's triggered ability fires as it enters the board, those triggered abilities are placed on the chain as pending items after the unit has already entered. [ 383.4.a.2 ] [ 383.2.c ] [ 383.3 ] Once those pending items are finalized with no further items pending, priority passes and players may react [ 337.4 ] — but by that point, the unit is already in play.

question: Can I play a reaction after one, but not all, items on the chain have resolved?
answer: Yes, once you have gained priority. The chain does not have to resolve in its entirety prior to (re)gaining priority, unlike in some other TCGs. Any time the most recent item on the chain resolves and there are no pending items, the controller of the newest item on the chain gains priority. [ 340.4 ] Example You put Singularity on the chain targeting an opponent's unit. Your opponent reacts by putting their Wind Wall on the chain, attempting to counter the Singularity. In response, you play Stupefy , in the hopes of drawing into a counterspell of your own. Once Stupefy resolves and you draw a card, priority is back to your opponent as the most recent item is their Wind Wall. After they pass priority, you can react once again and play your own counterspell, assuming you drew it off of the Stupefy. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: What does "play" mean on a card?
answer: "Play" refers to the same underlying action, but rules text uses it in three contexts that initiate or check that action at different points. [ 419.1 ] [ 419.4 ] In trigger conditions — "When you play," as seen on Ravenbloom Student and Darius, Trifarian — it means resolve. These abilities trigger once playing the card is complete, which happens at its resolution. [ 419.4 ] [ 419.4.a ] For units and gear, that's the instant they're finalized, since both resolve immediately without priority being passed; [ 337.2 ] for spells, resolution is a separate, later step, reached only after finalization and any reactions have played out. [ 339.1 ] [ 340.1 ] In conditional statements checking whether a card has been played — "if you've played," as seen on Battering Ram and Crescent Guardian — it means finalize, not resolve. A card satisfies this check when it becomes a finalized chain item. [ 329.3 ] The Legion keyword makes this precise: it's written as "if you have played another card this turn," [ 812.1.b.1 ] but the dependent ability is active as long as that other card "has been Finalized by you on the same turn" — not resolved. [ 812.1.c ] As an instruction — "play a card," as seen on Here to Help and Fizz, Trickster — it initiates that underlying action by placing the card on the chain and queuing it for finalization.
