question: When does a showdown close?
answer: Under normal game procedure, a showdown does not close abruptly. It ends once all players have consecutively passed focus on an empty chain. [ 348 ] Example You control a battlefield with a 2 might Stalwart Poro on it. Your opponent moves their Ravenbloom Student into that battlefield starting a showdown. When combat opens, Stalwart Poro becomes a defender and its Shield increases its might to 3. Once your opponent gains focus, they play Hextech Ray targeting Stalwart Poro. Hextech Ray resolves, marking 3 damage on it. During the resulting cleanup, Stalwart Poro is killed for lethal damage. [ 323.5 ] The showdown does not end right away and you gain focus as usual. You still have the opportunity to play a legally timed card or ability in an attempt to prevent your opponent from conquering. [ 347.1 ]

question: What happens when I move a unit into a non-combat showdown?
answer: When a unit controlled by a different player becomes present during a non-combat showdown, combat is staged and the showdown becomes a combat showdown during the cleanup following that unit's arrival. [ 316.8.b.1.a ] [ 323.9 ] [ 323.14 ] As combat opens, the player who originally applied contested status to the battlefield becomes the attacker, [ 464.2.c.1 ] and the player who moves in during the showdown becomes the defender. [ 464.2.c.2 ] Their units at that battlefield receive the corresponding designations then, [ 464.2.c.3 ] enabling combat-related keywords such as Assault and Shield and causing attack or defend triggers to happen. This interaction is commonly called the surprise defender: the player who first contested the battlefield remains the attacker, while the player joining later becomes the defender.

question: When do attack/defend triggers happen?
answer: Attack and defend triggered abilities (such as "When I attack" or "When I defend") trigger when a unit receives its attacker or defender designation, not necessarily at the start of combat. Units already present receive their initial designations when combat opens. [ 464.2.c.3 ] Units that join an ongoing combat receive their designations during the cleanup following their arrival.

question: Units can join combat late and still trigger
answer: If a unit is moved into a battlefield where combat is already in progress, it will receive the appropriate attacker or defender designation during the next cleanup. [ 323.2.a ] When it receives this designation, any "When I attack" or "When I defend" abilities will trigger at that time.

question: Attack and defend abilities only trigger once per combat
answer: Attack and defend triggered abilities can only trigger once per combat, even if a unit gains and loses its designation multiple times. [ 383.4.e.2.a ] [ 383.4.f.2.a ] Once a unit has been assigned an attacker or defender designation during a combat, moving it away from the battlefield will cause it to lose that designation. [ 323.2.c ] If that unit is moved back to the same battlefield during the same combat, it will gain the same designation as its controller, [ 323.2.a ] which will be the same designation it previously had. However, its "When I attack" or "When I defend" ability will not trigger again, as these abilities can only be fulfilled once per combat. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . question: What makes something a target?
answer: Unless one of the exceptions below applies, a game object, player, or zone mentioned by a spell or ability is a target. [ 355.7 ] [ 355.10 ] All targets are declared during finalization. [ 355.8 ] Card text does not need to use the word "target" or "choose" explicitly — targeting can be implied, as in "Kill a unit" or "Move a friendly unit." Abilities that reference "when you choose" a game object, such as Irelia, Fervent 's "When you choose or ready me, give me +1 Might this turn," are specifically triggered when being targeted. [ 383.4.b.3 ] When in doubt, assume it is a target — the list below covers the only situations where it is not: It is in a non-public zone (hand, main deck, etc.) [ 355.10.a ] e.g., "You may play a unit from your hand" does not target a unit — it merely lets you play one. It is only a location requirement for another target . [ 355.10.b ] Words like "at a battlefield" narrow down which objects are valid targets; the battlefield itself is not a target — unless the effect lets you choose which of several battlefields to affect, as in "Kill all units at a battlefield." It is part of a trigger condition, cost, or replacement effect . [ 355.10.c ] [ 355.10.c.1 ] Objects referenced in "when X happens" conditions, payment costs (see also When do I pay costs within instructions using "may"? ), or "instead" effects are not targets. e.g., the dying unit in "When a friendly unit dies, kill a gear" is not a target — only the gear is. There is no real choice involved . [ 355.10.d ] If an effect applies to every object meeting a description rather than a specific one you pick, nothing is targeted. e.g., "Kill all units at battlefields" targets nothing because you are not choosing among individual units. This applies only when a choice is never possible — not when an object merely happens to be the only valid choice right now: "Kill a unit at a battlefield" still targets a unit even if only one unit is there. [ 355.10.d.1 ] [ 355.10.d.2 ] It is part of a set chosen wholly or partly by other players . [ 355.10.e ] Objects chosen this way are not targets, even if the spell or ability's controller also chooses part of the set. e.g., "Each player kills a unit they control" targets nothing — each player chooses their unit as the effect resolves. The instruction uses "must" . [ 355.10.f ] This signals the choice is made on resolution rather than upfront. e.g., "You must recycle one of your runes" does not target, whereas "Recycle a rune you control" does. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: Can I use Ambush to play a unit to my base?
answer: No. Ambush only permits playing a unit to a battlefield; it has no effect on your base. Ambush is shorthand for "I may be played to a battlefield where you control units" and "I have Reaction as long as I'm being played to a battlefield where you control units." [ 822.1.b ] The permission Ambush grants is strictly limited to battlefields — a base is not a battlefield, so Ambush never makes it a valid destination. [ 822.1.c ] Playing a unit to your base is already permitted by the default rules for valid locations, [ 355.2.a ] but choosing base does not grant the unit Reaction . It can be played there only at its normal timing.

question: Can opponents react to a unit being played with Ambush?
answer: No. Ambush grants the unit Reaction speed, which determines when it can be played — it does not create a window for opponents to respond before the unit enters. Units resolve the moment they are finalized without entering the Execute step, [ 337.2 ] and finalization does not pass priority. [ 337.1.a ] The unit enters the board immediately, just as any unit played during an open state would (see also Can I react to units being played? ). This is a common point of confusion with cards like Kha'Zix, Mutating Horror , which has Ambush and triggers if an enemy unit is alone when he attacks or defends. An opponent cannot play a unit in response to Kha'Zix being placed on the chain in an attempt to break the "alone" condition before he enters.

question: Who gets to act after I Ambush a unit during a showdown?
answer: It depends on whether anything else remains on the chain once the unit enters. When played onto an empty chain, the unit enters immediately, the chain empties, and the turn returns to an open state during the showdown — focus passes to the next player in turn order. [ 340.2.a ] This catches many players off guard — you move in to attack, Ambush a unit, and expect to retain focus, but your opponent gets to act first. When played in response to something already on the chain — such as attack or defend triggers, or a spell — the turn does not return to an open state after the unit resolves, so focus does not pass. [ 346 ] Priority instead passes to the controller of the newest remaining item on the chain. [ 340.4 ] How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 19 July 2026 .

question: What happens to attached equipment when a unit dies?
answer: The equipment detaches and remains at the unit's last location, recalling if at a battlefield. When a unit with attached equipment dies, the equipment detaches and remains at the location the unit occupied before dying. [ 719.5 ] [ 435.4.b ] If that location is a battlefield, the detached equipment will be recalled to its controller's base during the next cleanup. [ 435.4.a ] If that location is the controller's base, the equipment simply remains there.

question: What happens to attached equipment when you take control of an enemy unit?
answer: Equipment stays attached but its controller does not change — only the top-most unit's controller changes. When you take control of a unit, any equipment attached to it retains its current controller. Changes in control of the top-most card do not affect control of attached cards, and vice versa. [ 718.5.f ] When the equipment detaches, it remains at the unit's last location. [ 719.5 ] [ 435.4.b ] If that location is a battlefield, it is recalled to its controller's base during the next cleanup. [ 435.4.a ] If that location is another player's base, the equipment remains there until the next cleanup, when it is recalled to its controller's base. [ 323.7 ] Because the equipment remains under the other player's control, that player can play a unit with Weaponmaster and choose the equipment, even while it is attached to the unit you control. [ 718.5.b ] [ 821.1.c ] If its Equip cost can be paid and it can legally be detached and attached, it moves to the newly played unit. [ 821.1.c.4 ] [ 821.1.c.5 ]

question: Which equipment effects choose units?
answer: Equip and Quick-Draw choose units; Weaponmaster does not. Some abilities trigger or care about when you choose friendly units. Here's how equipment-related effects interact with such abilities: When you activate a gear's Equip ability, you choose a unit you control to attach the equipment to. [ 818.1.b.1 ] This choice is a target, so activating Equip counts as choosing a unit. [ 355.7 ] When you play a gear with Quick-Draw , its triggered ability instructs you to "attach it to a Unit you control". [ 819.1.d ] While attaching cards doesn't inherently choose or specify a target, [ 434.3 ] Quick-Draw 's ability does require you to choose which unit to attach to. [ 355.10 ] This counts as choosing a unit. When you play a unit with Weaponmaster , you choose an equipment you control, not the unit. [ 821.1.c ] The rules explicitly state that "The Equip ability is not activated this way, and the unit with the Weaponmaster ability is not chosen". [ 821.1.c.6 ] Therefore, Weaponmaster does not count as choosing a unit.

question: Can I react to equipment abilities?
answer: Yes — all three equipment-related abilities create chain items that opponents can respond to before the attachment resolves. Equip is an activated ability. [ 818.1 ] Activated abilities use the chain, [ 377.3 ] so when you activate Equip , opponents have an opportunity to play a Reaction spell or ability before the attachment resolves. [ 377.3.b.2 ] When you play a Quick-Draw gear, the gear itself resolves immediately when finalized and cannot be reacted to. [ 337.2 ] However, Quick-Draw 's triggered ability — "When you play this, attach it to a unit you control" [ 819.1.d ] — is placed on the chain as a separate item. [ 383.4.a.2 ] Opponents can respond to that ability before the attachment resolves. Weaponmaster is also a triggered ability keyword. [ 821.1 ] Its ability triggers when you play the unit, and is placed on the chain just like any other triggered ability. [ 383.4.a.2 ] Opponents can respond to it before the equipment is attached. Skipping straight to attaching without checking for reactions is not correct play for any of these abilities. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) . Last updated on 20 July 2026 .

question: When do I decide whether to pay for Repeat?
answer: You must decide whether to pay a spell's Repeat cost when you play the spell, not later. When you play a spell with Repeat , you follow the normal process for playing a card: [ 353 ] First, you put the spell onto the chain [ 354 ] Then, you make relevant choices, [ 355 ] including whether or not you will pay its Repeat cost [ 355.1 ] [ 820.1.d ] Next, you determine its total cost. [ 356 ] If you chose to pay it, you apply the Repeat cost as an optional additional cost. [ 356.2.b.1 ] [ 820.1.d ] Finally, you complete the remaining steps of playing the card to finalize the spell This means you cannot put a spell on the chain, pass priority to see what happens, and then decide whether to pay its Repeat cost later. The decision must be made upfront during finalization. Any targets, modes, or other choices for the additional execution are also made during finalization and may differ from the original execution's choices. [ 820.2 ] [ 820.2.a ] Example You put Blood Rush , a spell with Repeat 1 , that says "Give a unit Assault 2 this turn," onto the chain. Before anyone can respond, you must decide whether to pay the 1 Repeat cost and choose the target for each execution. The two targets may be the same unit or different units. Once you've made this choice and paid costs, the spell is finalized. Your opponent can now respond with priority, but your Repeat decision is locked in.

question: What happens if a repeated spell is countered?
answer: The entire spell is countered, including all repeated instructions. Repeat does not create a second instance of the spell on the chain. [ 820.3.a ] Instead, it modifies how the spell resolves by executing its instructions an additional time. [ 820.1.d.1 ] When a spell is countered, it does nothing and is cleared from the chain. [ 425.1.a ] Since the spell never resolves, none of its instructions are executed, whether they came from Repeat or not. How was this page? Written by Christian I. (Near) .
